title: From the Military to Soaring Careers: A New Donation Clears the Runway for Other Transitioning Service Members
summary: Transitioning out of the military and into a civilian career takes more than training. That’s why GE Aerospace is making that step easier for more service members.
body_markdown:
Transitioning out of the military and into a civilian career takes more than training. That’s why GE Aerospace is making that step easier for more service members.


As Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University marks its 100th anniversary, GE Aerospace Chairman and CEO Larry Culp announced[a $100,000 donation](https://www.geaerospace.com/news/press-releases/ge-aerospace-commits-100k-embry-riddle-support-transitioning-service-members) to the school’s Aviation Maintenance Technology SkillBridge program, during the Presidential Speaker Series at the university’s Daytona Beach campus. The donation will help cover costs like tuition and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) testing expenses for transitioning service members in the program.


Bryan MacLean and Matthew Grassi are proof of where that transition can lead. Two service members who took very different routes out of the military, they share the same two names in their civilian careers: GE Aerospace and Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University.


**From the Flight Line to the Front of the Classroom**


MacLean spent nearly a decade in the Air Force, working on the C-5M Super Galaxy, one of the U.S. Air Force’s largest cargo aircraft, before an injury led to his medical retirement. A connection at Dover Air Force Base helped him land a job at GE Aerospace, where he started as a jet instructor for engineers. He enjoyed the work and wanted to advance, so he pursued a bachelor’s degree at Embry-Riddle, studying aviation maintenance management entirely online while working full-time — with a newborn at home.


“I would work and spend time with my family and spend about four hours every night doing homework,” MacLean says.


After retiring from the Air Force, Bryan MacLean earned his Embry-Riddle degree online while working full-time, building a career at GE Aerospace where he now teaches commercial engine maintenance to airline mechanics worldwide. Images credit: GE Aerospace


The coursework gave him context he’d never needed in uniform, from civil aviation regulation to the realities of working with international airline customers. “Since I started in aviation, I’ve learned something new every day,” MacLean says. “It’s such a big industry. There’s so much available.”


Today, MacLean is based in Cincinnati, where he works as a large commercial engine instructor, teaching 16 different engine classes to mechanics from major airlines worldwide. He also works alongside GE Aerospace’s engineering teams, testing new tooling before it reaches customers.


For anyone starting out in the industry or considering a move into it, MacLean’s advice is simple: “Be a sponge. Be willing to learn new things and network. The more people you know that can help you, the easier this is.”


**Keeping Black Hawks in the Air**


For MacLean, Embry-Riddle was a way up after he’d already joined GE Aerospace. For Grassi, it was the way in.


Grassi’s journey began in the Marine Corps, where he worked as an engine mechanic on heavy-lift helicopters. As he prepared to leave active duty, Embry-Riddle was running a SkillBridge transition course on his base in Jacksonville, North Carolina. The SkillBridge program lets transitioning service members use their final months in uniform to train with participating companies and schools for civilian careers. One of Embry-Riddle’s courses, offered on select military bases, focuses on general aviation maintenance, helping veterans work toward an airframe and powerplant certification before they leave the military.


Former Marine and GE Aerospace field service representative Matthew Grassi credits early mentorship and his degree from Embry-Riddle with helping him translate military experience into a successful civilian career.


“This man sat every one of us down,” Grassi says of his instructor, Dr. James Stockton. “He taught us how to write a structured paper, how to take our thoughts as active-duty Marines and transition them into the language of corporate America.”


That preparation became a foundation Grassi would rely on for years. He joined GE Aerospace and worked his way through several roles, beginning in engine testing, before moving into field service. Today he is the on-site field service representative at Sikorsky in Stratford, Connecticut. “I love my job,” he says.


This fall, he also completed his bachelor’s degree in aeronautics through Embry-Riddle, a milestone five years in the making since he left active duty.


Looking back on that journey, Grassi says progress isn’t always visible in the moment. “When you look back, starting years ago, I didn’t think I’d ever be where I am now,” he says. “But then you see progress, and that’s what motivates me to keep going.”


MacLean and Grassi are among more than 450 Embry-Riddle alumni who now work at GE Aerospace. Both found a career in aviation after the military, and GE Aerospace’s donation will help more service members do the same.
